extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in humor, literature, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A short popular-essay analysis of historical and philosophical theories of laughter (Hobbes and Hutcheson) and a personal synthesis explaining when and why people laugh. Focus is on causes of laughter (superiority, incongruity, and their interaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden Glory (Hobbes' superiority theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sudden Glory, is the passion which maketh those Grimaces we call LAUGHTER; and it is caused either by some sudden act of their own, that pleaseth them; or by the apprehension of some deformed thing in another, by comparison whereof they suddenly applaud themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter arises from a sudden feeling of superiority — either over another's deformity/fault or over a previous self. Examples: laughing at a know-nothing comic character (Stephen Colbert) where we occupy a superior informational position. Notes/limits: the theory is blunt and can be morally uncomfortable (it predicts laughing at others), and it does not by itself explain why we do not laugh at certain pitiable or tragic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory (Hutcheson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter comes from the perception of incongruity—specifically, the incongruity between 'ideas of grandeur, dignity, sanctity, perfection, and ideas of meanness, baseness, profanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We laugh when something dignified is juxtaposed with something undignified (e.g., the Pope farting) or when an elevated style is applied to a trivial subject (Pope's The Rape of the Lock). Hutcheson supplements this by positing an inherent human dignity, so undignified events that violate that dignity produce incongruity-based laughter. Limitations: incongruity can exist without producing laughter (see banal or tragic incongruities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic irony as a mechanism (knowledge-based superiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when we occupy a position of knowledge or awareness that a character does not — a form of superiority grounded in dramatic irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic effects where audience knowledge > character knowledge (Colbert's persona, many comic characters) produce laughter because we see the character's ignorance and feel superior. This is a specific application of the superiority/information asymmetry mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/empathic constraints on laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all superiority or incongruity occasions laughter; empathy and social/moral context can block laughter (e.g., 'the healthy don't generally laugh at the ill').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: we typically do not laugh at a homeless person coughing and begging; social position and compassion suppress the superiority impulse. Counterexample noted: callous social contexts (e.g., certain political fundraisers) may override empathy and produce laughter at others' misfortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity alone is not sufficient (banal vs tragic incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some incongruities are banal or tragic and therefore not funny (e.g., a green Post-It among yellow ones is banal; Sophocles' Oedipus has incongruity but is tragic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish comic incongruity from mere oddity or from tragic inversion; not every mismatch between expectations and reality yields humor. This is an anti-pattern for expecting incongruity always to produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined effect: incongruity plus (self-directed) superiority ('double whammy')
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can result from an interaction of incongruity and a special kind of superiority — including feeling superior to one's own prior self — producing a 'double whammy' effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's personal example: laughing at the idea of a 20th anniversary because of the clash between youthful self-image and middle-aged reality (incongruity) plus a momentary elevation above one's prior deluded self (self-directed superiority). Small everyday examples include realizing one has been angrily trying the wrong car key: the sudden elevation from delusion to realization triggers laughter. This synthesis explains laughter that neither Hobbes nor Hutcheson alone fully captures.
